subject: horse
title: What If a Horse Could Do Maths? In 1904, 13 Experts Said One Could

scenes.text: What if a horse could do arithmetic? In 1904, a panel of experts said one could.
His name was Clever Hans. His owner, a German maths teacher, asked him sums, and Hans tapped out the answers with his hoof.
Fractions, spelling, telling the time. A commission of thirteen experts investigated and found no trickery at all.
Then a psychologist, Oskar Pfungst, changed one thing. He made sure the person asking didn't know the answer.
Hans's score fell from 89 percent to 6. He couldn't count. He was reading people: they tensed as he neared the right number, and relaxed when he reached it.
Nobody was cheating, not even his owner. It's why scientists run blind experiments today, and it's still called the Clever Hans effect.

description:
What if an animal could really do maths? In Germany in the early 1900s a horse called Clever Hans appeared to add, divide, spell and tell the time by tapping his hoof, and in 1904 a commission of 13 experts found no trickery.
Psychologist Oskar Pfungst then showed that Hans was right 89 percent of the time when the questioner knew the answer and could be seen, but only 6 percent when the questioner did not know it. The horse was reading tiny, involuntary changes in posture and expression. The case led to blind experimental methods.

first_comment: Hans may not have done maths, but reading a human face that well is its own kind of clever. Which animal is smarter than we think, and what should we run through next?
